common_name: Early Amethyst Beautyberry (Compact Early-Fruiting Purple Beautyberry)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Early Amethyst is a compact selection of purple beautyberry that fruits earlier and more heavily than the species, with clusters of vivid violet-purple berries lining arching branches in fall.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Early Amethyst is a compact selection of Asian beautyberry prized for producing an especially heavy, early display of small, intensely violet-purple berries clustered tightly along graceful, arching branches in fall, after inconspicuous pink summer flowers. Its smaller mature size compared to native American beautyberry makes it a better fit for foundation plantings and smaller gardens, though the vivid fall berry display is just as striking. It flowers and fruits on new wood, so a hard pruning in late winter to a foot or two from the ground each year encourages the most vigorous new growth and heaviest berry set the following fall.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Issai is a dwarf beautyberry that sets fruit reliably even as a young plant, unlike some beautyberries that need a few seasons to bear heavily.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Issai is a compact, dwarf beautyberry selection that reliably sets heavy clusters of bright violet-purple berries even on young plants, without needing the several-year establishment period some beautyberries require before fruiting well. Its small mature size makes it a good fit for foundation plantings, mixed borders, and smaller gardens where the full-sized native American beautyberry would grow too large. It flowers and fruits on new wood, so cutting the shrub back hard to a foot or so from the ground each late winter encourages vigorous new growth and the heaviest berry production the following fall.

common_name: Blue Muffin Viburnum (Compact Native Arrowwood with Heavy Blue Berries)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Blue Muffin is a compact arrowwood viburnum selected for unusually heavy production of vivid blue berries, and planting a second unrelated arrowwood clone nearby improves fruit set.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade, ideally with a different arrowwood viburnum clone nearby to improve cross-pollination and berry set. Blue Muffin is a compact selection of native arrowwood viburnum bred specifically for heavy, reliable production of vivid, deep blue berries in fall, a standout food source for birds and a striking ornamental display against the shrub's red-purple fall foliage. Its smaller mature size compared to the wild species fits foundation plantings, mixed borders, and hedgerows where a full-sized arrowwood would need more room. It is highly adaptable to a range of soil conditions from dry to moist and needs only occasional structural pruning to maintain shape.

common_name: Winterthur Viburnum (Compact Possumhaw with Multi-Season Berry Color)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Winterthur is a compact possumhaw viburnum selection with berries that shift through pink, blue, and near-black as they ripen, all often visible on the same cluster at once.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to occasionally wet, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; possumhaw viburnum is one of the best viburnums for wet or poorly drained sites, including rain gardens and pond margins. Winterthur is a compact selection of native possumhaw viburnum producing showy clusters of berries that pass through a striking sequence of pink, blue, and near-black as they ripen in late summer and fall, often displaying several colors on the same cluster at once, in addition to attractive burgundy-red fall foliage. Its smaller stature compared to the species fits typical residential borders better, and planting a second unrelated clone nearby improves the reliability and abundance of berry set.

common_name: Thomas Edison Dahlia (Classic Large Deep Purple Dahlia)

planting.note: Plant tubers horizontally 4-6 inches deep after last frost; Thomas Edison is a classic large decorative dahlia producing huge, fully double, deep royal purple blooms on a tall, sturdy plant that benefits from staking.

directions: Plant tubers horizontally, four to six inches deep, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun after the last frost. Thomas Edison is a long-cherished large decorative dahlia cultivar, producing huge, fully double flowers in a rich, deep royal purple that hold their color well and make outstanding, long-lasting cut flowers. The tall, vigorous plants benefit from staking to support the heavy flower heads, and pinching the growing tip when young encourages a bushier plant with more flowering stems. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with good drainage and heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler zones ensures the most reliable survival from year to year.
